newsitem.title: JAPAN: Policy agreement of Japan's new alliance.
newsitem.headline: Policy agreement of Japan's new alliance.

text.p: Here is the gist of a policy agreement issued by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and leaders of other parties in his new political alliance launched on Thursday.
The document was signed by Hashimoto, leader of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), Social Democratic Party leader Takako Doi and Akiko Domoto of the Sakigake Party:

- Administrative reform: The three parties will work towards reform of central government ministries, with a bill to be drafted by next September. The council overseeing this will be formed under the leadership of a person outside politics and the bureaucracy. The bill will be submitted in the regular January-June parliament session of 1998.
- Parliament: The alliance will work towards reducing parliamentary seats and set up a watchdog group to oversee the conduct of the civil service.

- Finance Ministry and Bank of Japan: The alliance will aim to set up a body to oversee financial institutions separate from the Finance Ministry, and seek to strengthen the independence of the central bank. Bills will be submitted in the regular parliament to be convened in January.

- Sales Tax: The alliance will set up a special parliamentary committee in the next extraordinary session to review the tax system. The sales tax, a three-percent value-added levy on all goods and services, will be raised to five percent next April. The Social Democrats have been calling for foodstuffs to be exempted from the increase, saying a higher consumption tax would have a negative impact on the poor.
- Nursing-the-Aged Law: The alliance will submit a bill in the next extraordinary session of parliament to introduce a public system of nursing for the elderly.
- Volunteer Law: The alliance will submit a bill in the next regular parliament to enable workers to take part in volunteer programmes without using their vacation time.

- Foreign policy and security issues: The alliance agreed to conduct an Asian foreign policy reaffirming former Prime Minister Tomiichi Murayama's 1995 communique expressing remorse for Japan's actions in World War Two and promote regional disarmament and security dialogues. The alliance will adhere to the constitutional ban on entering a collective (offensive) security arrangement when drafting a new set of military guidelines under the 1960 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty and make efforts to avoid misunderstanding on the nature of the new guidelines among Asian neighbours. (The review is to be conducted in December).
The three parties failed to agree on the following issues but will continue discussions on them. They were also listed in the policy document:

- Political donations: The Social Democratic Party proposed an immediate, blanket ban on political donations from private firms and institutions, such as trade unions and religious groups. The LDP promised to consider the ban.
- Okinawa: The Social Democrats proposed starting formal talks with the United States to reduce U.S. troops on the southern island, which houses a U.S. Marine Corps division. The LDP rejected this.

- Status of (U.S.) Forces: The Social Democrats proposed drafting a new Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) that defines the legal status of U.S. troops in Japan. SOFA became an issue when three Okinawa-based U.S. servicemen were arrested for raping an Okinawan schoolgirl last year and were subsequently convicted. The LDP said the application of SOFA should be improved, not the document itself.
- Reduction of the defence budget: The Social Democrats proposed some cuts in Japan's $50 billion defence outlay. The LDP said the government has already set a ceiling in the current five-year plan.

- The LDP also rejected Social Democratic Party proposals that include the hosting of a nuclear disarmament conference in Hiroshima and new laws to empower parliament to inspect government aid for developing countries, to enable married women to retain their family names, and to conduct local referendums when constructing nuclear power plants.
